content: Aramid fibers are a category of synthetic fibers known for their exceptional heat resistance and mechanical strength. These fibers are widely utilized in aerospace and military applications, including ballistic-rated body armor fabrics, and as a substitute for asbestos. The term aramid is derived from aromatic polyamide, reflecting their chemical structure. The molecular chains in aramid fibers are highly oriented along the fiber axis, allowing the chemical bonds to contribute significantly to their strength. Aromatic polyamides were first introduced for commercial use in the early 1960s. DuPont developed the meta-aramid fiber known as Nomex, which remains a highly heat-resistant material used in thermal and electrical insulation. Other manufacturers, such as Teijin (under the trade name Teijinconex) and Kermel in Europe, also began producing similar materials in the 1970s. Building on earlier research by Monsanto and Bayer, DuPont and Akzo Nobel developed fibers with significantly higher tenacity and elastic modulus during the 1960s and 1970s, leveraging their expertise in rayon, polyester, and nylon processing. Stephanie Kwolek, a scientist at DuPont, made significant contributions to the development of aramid fibers in 1961. DuPont introduced the para-aramid fiber Kevlar in 1973, which became a groundbreaking material. A similar para-aramid fiber, Twaron, with a comparable chemical structure, was introduced by Akzo in 1978. However, due to prior patents on the production process, a patent dispute arose between Akzo and DuPont in the 1980s. Twaron is now owned by the Teijin company. Aramid fibers are employed in numerous high-tech applications, including aerospace and military uses, bulletproof body armor fabrics, and as replacements for asbestos. According to the Federal Trade Commission, aramid fibers are defined as manufactured fibers in which the fiber-forming substance is a long-chain synthetic polyamide, with at least 85% of the amide linkages (-CO-NH-) directly attached to two aromatic rings. The production of aramid fibers involves the reaction between an amine group and a carboxylic acid halide group. The most well-known aramids, such as Nomex, Kevlar, and Twaron, are AA-BB polymers. Nomex and Teijinconex predominantly contain meta-linkages and are classified as poly-metaphenylene isophthalamides (MPIA). Kevlar and Twaron, on the other hand, are para-aramids composed of p-phenylene terephthalamide (PPTA), the simplest form of AA-BB para-polyaramide. PPTA is synthesized from p-phenylene diamine (PPD) and terephthaloyl dichloride (TDC or TCl). The production of PPTA relies on a co-solvent system, which includes calcium chloride (CaCl2) to disrupt hydrogen bonds in the amide groups and N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP) to dissolve the aromatic polymer. This process, developed by Leo Vollbracht at the Dutch chemical firm Akzo, was a significant advancement, as no practical method for dissolving the polymer was previously known. The introduction of this system also led to a patent dispute between Akzo and DuPont. After the polymer is produced, aramid fibers are created through a spinning process, where the dissolved polymer is transformed into solid fibers from a liquid chemical blend. For spinning PPTA, the polymer solvent typically used is 100% anhydrous sulfuric acid (H2SO4). Aramid fibers are available in various forms, including continuous fibers, chopped fibers, powders, and pulps. Beyond meta-aramids like Nomex, other variations of aramid fibers exist, primarily of the copolyamide type. One notable example is Technora, developed by Teijin and introduced in 1976. The manufacturing process for Technora involves reacting PPD and 3,4'-diaminodiphenyl ether (3,4'-ODA) with terephthaloyl chloride (TCl). This relatively straightforward process uses only one amide solvent, allowing spinning to occur directly after polymer production. Aramid fibers exhibit a high degree of molecular orientation, a characteristic shared with other advanced fibers like ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene. This orientation significantly influences their properties. Aramid fibers are challenging to dye and are typically solution-dyed during production. Major industrial applications of aramid fibers include flame-resistant clothing, heat-protective garments and helmets, and body armor. In the body armor sector, aramid fibers compete with polyethylene-based fiber products such as Dyneema and Spectra.
